rv.q: Even more strikingly, Omari Douglas and Russell Tovey, as a same-sex couple, find multiple possibilities in this piece about multiple possibilities.
It is hard to imagine it better performed than on these starry, starry nights.

This play manifests its science organically in both form and content, applying its quantum physics to the human drama with fantastic imagination, and playing with formal non-linearity with no sense of shallowness or gimmickry.
This is a short, sharp, smart hit of first-class drama, that humanises the randomness of the universe.
Douglas and Tovey’s same-sex version is perhaps the richest yet.
Atim is a complete five-star joy to watch: hilarious, angry and vulnerable, and Jeremiah her bewildered on-off partner.
Their pairing lands Payne’s beautifully measured unpeeling of the many layers of who we are (and can be) in a big, bold terrain.
It’s astonishing how much quality drama Payne manages to capture in just 75 minutes.
Constellations is by far the classiest offering currently on show in a West End that remains some way from full strength – and Atim, for one, is a shooting star.
It’s a zingy, entertaining play.
It's a beguiling 70 minutes that could run and run, with different actors, in a pan-cosmic groundhog day.
Standout performer Sheila Atim has the gift of making every line feel like it was written just for her.
This story, raw for too many of us, should be moving, but sentiment is impeded by Payne's tricksy narrative that keeps stopping and rewinding.
But neither couple quite captures the precision of delivery or the sheer emotional heft that Rafe Spall and Sally Hawkins brought to Longhurst’s original Royal Court staging.
Constellations's ever-shifting form and its mix of science, faith, and love remains as spry and sparkling as it was nine years ago.
This revival of Nick Payne's contemplative and ingenious Constellations is smart, funny and exceptionally moving.
The new acting teams are stunning, and turn what was previously a fine piece of theatre into an unmissable theatrical event: if you have the time and the money, try to see them both.
Michael Longhurst's revival of Nick Payne's 2012. Constellations is one of the most polished and precise productions I've ever seen.
This adds a further layer of fluidity to Payne’s vulnerable and enriching tragi-comedy.

Director Michael Longhurst deserves acclaim for achieving such integrity and emotional balance in such contrasting casts and readings – and both pairs wring immense entertainment out of Payne's light-penned script.
This ingenious revival, by original director Michael Longhust, offers four casts — and yet more variations.
This new format fits the play so well it’s surprising somebody hasn’t tried it before.
No matter which cast of Constellations they see, it’s a theatrical experience that is out of this world.
This is because Constellations is one of those plays whose brilliance lies in its structure rather than what is said by or happens to its characters.

cn.t: Critics hail Payne's ingenious multiverse romance as smart, moving, and dazzlingly structured, with the four-cast concept brilliantly amplifying its themes of infinite possibility. A few find the fragmented storytelling gimmicky, but most praise its emotional depth.
